cells.tense: You are keeping a direction alight at this moment, with the pen still in your hand.
cells.act: envision it freshly and feel toward it
cells.ask: Picture the step past the one you're on. Feel toward it before you plan it. Two minutes, then back to the desk.
cells.core:
You can keep a fire going without burning yourself out, and that is what's happening. The direction you're holding is real, the pace is one you could keep for a long while, and the ones working beside you can feel the flame is neither rationed nor flaring. Steadiness like this is what the whole thing runs on.

Because you've let your experience settle instead of racing it, there is room now to look ahead without flinching. Spend two minutes on it: see the next step, feel your way toward it, no plan attached. Then come back. That kind of seeing is what your slower work bought you, and it keeps the direction from going flat.
cells.sheetLine: The fire is steady — you can afford to look ahead.
cells.verb: tending a fire that has to keep burning while you keep your footing
cells.place: the stretch of road that holds a direction through resistance

cells.tense: You are bracing at a future you cannot write in from here.
cells.act: calibrate what you say to what can be heard
cells.ask: Before the next plan talk, catch whether it's for the one listening or just for your own nerves. Say one sentence you'd stand behind if nothing changed. Let the rest wait.
cells.core:
You're running hot for something that hasn't happened. The next move gets walked through in your head so many times that the walking-through starts to feel like progress. You keep the flame, and that keeping has outgrown what the flame needs.

The friction isn't your commitment. Some of what you say about the plan is aimed at steadying yourself rather than at the person sitting with you. Say one sentence you'd stand behind if nothing changed, and let it land. The vision doesn't have to shrink; it just has to touch ground where a real move could happen. When the direction comes out of what you honestly feel, the pacing quiets by itself.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that shut behind you a while back.
cells.ask: Look at the work still on your shoulders and ask what it's for. If the honest answer is 'the person who began it', release a piece. Not the whole.
cells.core:
Directed motion used to be simple for you: something pulled you out of bed, the pace was yours, and you held the course through resistance without being eaten by it. That is how this goes when it goes well. It isn't going that way now. The engine that once pulled you forward is quiet, and part of you keeps waiting by the old route for it to come back.

What brings the direction back isn't pushing harder into the quiet. Release one finished thing exactly as it is, and the way forward shows itself. You don't have to feel driven before you clear what's done. Clear the finished weight, and the appetite follows.
cells.sheetLine: The fuel you're missing is the weight still on your back.

cells.tense: You are steering something at this moment without counting yourself as the one at the wheel.
cells.act: move the structure one real inch
cells.ask: Make one small part of the change you describe as happening to you happen by hand this week. One form, one message, one physical shift.
cells.core:
A healthy version of this has a direction unmistakably your own. You wake pointed at something, you move on it without waiting for the mood to show up, and the ones beside you get the benefit of that steadiness. You can hold a course through pushback and still treat yourself decently while you do it.

What's bending it out of shape is quieter. You are already moving something, steady, week after week, but you file it under the situation, or the way things are shaking out. The effort is real. The hand making it happen belongs to you, and you don't count it that way.
cells.sheetLine: You are doing the pushing and calling it the situation.
